Patient Vignette: Maria

Maria is a 53-year-old married woman of Latin American descent who has worked as a stock broker for over twenty years. She presents as impeccably dressed, with a sharp, direct manner that initially seems to keep me at a professional distance. Her story unfolds slowly, in fragments, over our first few sessions.

It happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late November. Maria had stayed late at her office in the financial district, reviewing fourth-quarter projections. The building was emptying out, the winter sky already dark. She remembers feeling a familiar, pleasant fatigue - the exhaustion of a good day's work. As she walked the two blocks to the parking garage, she was checking her phone, scrolling through her daughter's college application updates.

She never heard him approach. The first thing she felt was the cold, hard circle of a gun barrel pressed against the back of her skull. "Give me the bag, or I will blow your head off." The voice was young, almost a boy's voice, but flat and practiced. Maria froze. She handed over her leather tote - her laptop, her phone, her wallet with the family photos, her grandmother's silver rosary. He shoved her hard, and she fell, scraping her palms on the concrete. He ran. The whole thing took maybe forty-five seconds.

In the immediate aftermath, Maria was praised for her composure. She reported the crime, gave a statement, and drove herself home. She told her husband, Carlos, that she was fine, just shaken. She took the next day off, worked from home the day after that. She was a professional. She knew how to handle volatility.

But the market inside her was crashing.

The first symptom she noticed was the scanning. At her desk, she cannot sit with her back to the door. She has rearranged her entire corner office so she can see the entrance and the hallway. Every time a colleague walks by, her heart lurches. She has stopped taking the elevator; the enclosed space feels like a trap. She takes the stairs, all fourteen floors, twice a day. Her knees ache, but she cannot stop.

The hypervigilance has bled into everything. She now parks in the most expensive, well-lit lot, even though it cuts into her monthly bonus. She walks with her keys fisted between her knuckles, a habit she saw on a true crime documentary. The sound of a car backfiring on the street makes her drop to a crouch. Last month, at a celebratory dinner for a huge IPO, a waiter dropped a tray of glasses. Maria screamed, then excused herself to the restroom, where she vomited.

She is having trouble sleeping. Not just falling asleep, but staying asleep. She wakes at 3:17 a.m. every single night - the exact time the police report was filed. Her mind immediately goes to the sensation of the metal on her scalp. She feels it, phantom-like, even now as she tells me the story, and she touches the back of her head with her palm.

Her marriage is strained. Carlos wants to help, but Maria has become irritable and distant. She snapped at him last week for walking up behind her in the kitchen. "You scared me to death!" she yelled. She sees the hurt in his eyes, but she cannot apologize. She feels a constant, low-level rage, not at the young man who robbed her - she has already imagined shooting him in her mind, a hundred times - but at herself. She is furious that she froze. She is a broker. She makes split-second decisions worth millions. How could she have just stood there?

Her work, once a source of pride, is now a minefield. She cannot concentrate. She reads the same line of a quarterly report five times. She missed a critical stop-loss order last month, costing a client a significant sum. Her boss has noticed. He asked if she was "okay." She said she was fine.

Yesterday, for the first time in eight months, she took the subway. She got one stop before the panic hit - the walls closing in, the air thick, the faces around her blurring into potential threats. She bolted off the train at 42nd Street and stood on the platform, shaking. She hasn't told anyone that part yet. She is terrified that if she tells her boss, he will take her off the active trading desk. And she does not know who she is if she is not trading.
